title: Opening the doors to a rich curriculum
author: Mary Myatt
summary: Mary Myatt describes how the Compass Eko Trust, a group of twenty-eight schools across southern England, set out to build a genuinely rich curriculum for pupils with the most complex needs. Leaders found that timetables packed with specialist support and interventions had left these pupils with a drastically reduced curriculum. Observation in the trust's special schools showed that learning was anchored in subjects such as science, history, art and music, which gave context for communication, shared attention and curiosity. To make this workable in mainstream schools, special school practitioners worked with subject leaders and SENCOs to map the National Curriculum across three developmental profiles, starting with a bounded science rollout and a single planning day. The project also challenged assumptions about inclusion, since sitting in the same room is not the same as meaningful participation in worthwhile knowledge. Myatt concludes that the starting question should shift from whether a child can manage the standard worksheet to what the subject makes possible for them.
points: Well-intentioned specialist support can crowd out the wider curriculum, so leaders need to look at a pupil's whole week rather than each intervention in isolation.
Subjects are the vehicle through which development happens for pupils with complex needs, rather than an extra hurdle on top of therapy goals.
A bounded rollout, a single planning day and specialist colleagues alongside teachers dissolved mainstream teachers' fear of getting it wrong.
Mapping the National Curriculum across three developmental profiles gave teachers a practical structure instead of a diluted version of standard lessons.
Real inclusion means meaningful participation in worthwhile knowledge, not simply being present in the classroom with a teaching assistant.
quotes: Each component had good intentions behind it. Yet when leaders stepped back to look at the week as a whole, the reality was uncomfortable.
In trying to meet every specific need, these pupils had been handed a drastically reduced curriculum.

Learning was not organised around generic sensory exercises; it was anchored in subjects. Science, history, geography, art and music provided the context for communication, shared attention and curiosity.
The subject is not an extra hurdle. It is the vehicle through which development happens.
Transplanting a special school model wholesale was never going to work, nor was simply diluting standard lessons.
That bounded task was important because when teachers feel hesitant about teaching pupils with complex needs, it is rarely due to a lack of care. They are simply worried about getting it wrong.

Sitting in the same physical room as twenty-nine other children does not mean a pupil is included. A child can sit at the back with a teaching assistant and still be completely cut off from the subject.
We stop asking whether a child can manage the standard worksheet. We ask what the subject itself makes possible for them, and how we can open the door.
